title: Open engagement in Berlin and Lenidow's first jazz venture
summary: The Berlin run was open ended, extended by demand to around seventy performances, for the impresario's first venture into jazz.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You were held over in Berlin, weren't you, at that theater.
Oh, yes. Because at the time it was unknown when we hit Berlin. It was unknown. I mean there was no known quantity of time that we was supposed to have.

They kept coming, and people just kept coming. And we kept setting back dates. Setting back other dates. As long as they could pull us out of Berlin. Because Berlin was the major city and at the same time they were putting the propaganda out, how great we were.
Well, Leonidow was a very big impresario. Didn't he handle Chaliapin and people like that, opera singers.
Yes. This was his first venture into --

And I guess maybe he could have come over here because he was a very close friend of Hurok's, you know. Then later on they did a lot of work together and we had a second "Chocolate Kitties" with he and Hurok. See both of them were from Russia together. I think that they had been kids in Russia at the same time. So he knew that, but this was his first venture. And so far, it was his greatest.
And you were actually, then, when you opened in Berlin, you were already booked for other cities, or other countries, or what? Was it supposed to be a whole tour?
Not too far. Because he wasn't sure of it.

See, there hadn't been any -- an event like this preceeding this. We didn't know what was going to happen. You see he was taking a chance and he was scareder than we were. He was scared to death. But, if it was a success -- the next place, I think, was Sweden.
So he was feeling his way with you.
But you stayed in Berlin for quite awhile, didn't you?
Oh, yeah. I think it was about 70 or 73
